fields.connection: V plain form + ばかりか / N / Na + な / Aい
examples: His research is attracting attention not only in Japan but also from overseas.
The restaurant I went to yesterday wasn't good, and on top of that it was expensive. I never want to go there again.
Not only my parents but also my older sister opposed my studying abroad.
I have no money, so not only can I not go on a trip, I can't even eat out.
The queen was not only beautiful but also kind-hearted.
Not only is this vegetable rich in vitamins, it also helps prevent cancer.
fields.explain:
◎ An expression showing surprise, "not only that," and bringing up something else.
◎ It has the same meaning as「～ばかりなく」, but this expression is usually used in written language.
fields.notes:
meaning_vi: Not only… but also… | Not only…, but also
explain: Used when B is unexpected and stronger than A in its positive/negative degree.
The style leans toward writing and presentations; in speech, ～だけでなく/～に加えて are common.
To emphasize an extreme degree, use まで/さえ in the second clause: ～ばかりか～まで/さえ.
Keep the two clauses parallel in word type (N—N; clause—clause) so it sounds natural.
The subject usually stays the same in both clauses; if it changes, make it clear to avoid ambiguity.
examples: 1. 彼は日本語ばかりか、フランス語も話せる。
He can speak not only Japanese but also French.
2. この冬は寒いばかりか、雪も多かった。
This winter was not only cold but also had a lot of snow.
3. その店は値段が高いばかりか、店員の態度も悪い。
That shop is not only expensive, but the staff's attitude is bad too.
4. 彼女は歌ばかりか、ダンスもプロ並みだ。
She is at a professional level not only in singing but also in dancing.
5. 事故で車ばかりか、荷物も壊れてしまった。
In the accident, not only the car but also the luggage was damaged.
──────
1. 彼は日本語ばかりか、英語も話せる。
He can speak not only Japanese but also English.
2. この店は値段が高いばかりか、サービスも悪い。
This shop is not only expensive, but the service is bad too.
3. 大雨で試合ばかりか、授業も中止になった。
Because of the heavy rain, not only the game but also classes were canceled.
4. 彼女は歌ばかりか、踊りも上手だ。
She is good not only at singing but also at dancing.
5. そればかりか、交通費まで出してくれた。
Not only that, they even paid for my transportation.
6. 手伝ってくれないばかりか、文句まで言う。
Not only do they not help, they even complain.
meaning_vi: Not only…but also…
explain: Used to show that a thing or matter has an additional (bad) characteristic besides the one already known
Expresses annoyance, disappointment, dissatisfaction
examples: 1. あの店は、味が悪いばかりか、店員の態度もひどい。
At that shop, not only is the food bad, but the staff's attitude is terrible too
2. 私は、漢字ばかりか、まだひらがなも書けません。
I can't write not only kanji but even hiragana yet
meaning_vi: Not only ～, in addition…
explain: Expresses the meaning "not only ～ but also…"　Adds something of greater scope or degree.
Sentences of command or compulsion are almost never used after 「ばかりか／ばかりでなく」
examples: 1. あの人は、学校の成績がいいばかりかスボーツもできる。
That person not only has good grades at school but is also good at sports.
2. このあたりは、空気ばかりでなく水も汚染されている。
Around here, not only the air but also the water is polluted.
mistakes: Dropping も in the second clause: you need ～も/まで/さえ for the correct nuance of "unexpected addition."
Reversing the degree: putting the stronger information in A and the weaker in B weakens the rhetorical effect.
Confusing it with ～だけでなく when the question calls for a nuance of "unexpected/more serious" → choose ～ばかりか.
Overusing it with two different subjects makes the sentence ambiguous; prefer the same subject.

examples: Just because I told someone else the secret, I ended up making her angry.
Just because I missed the deadline for the report, I didn't get the credits.
Just because I was late, I ended up causing trouble for everyone.
Just because I believed one thing he said, I had a terrible time.
Just because I'm tall, I stand out wherever I go.
Just because my older brother is quiet, he often seems to be misunderstood as a cold person.
fields.explain:
Suits contexts of regret, justification and complaint.
With “V-たい＋ばかりに”: emphasizes an excessive motive; may imply self-blame.
Not used for a neutral, objective cause (in that case ～ために/ので is more natural).

• Just because… , …: A single cause leads to a result (often negative/regrettable). Implies resentment or regret.
• Just to… , …: Because of a single desire/motive, someone does an action (sometimes recklessly/not worth it).
• Evaluation: The speaker judges the cause as trivial or simple, yet it has major consequences.
fields.notes:
• Written language prefers “N/Aである＋ばかりに” to raise formality.
• When the subject suffers harm: often used with ～てしまう／～ことになった to emphasize that it was unavoidable.
• Cause phrases of the “appearance” type can also be used: 見た目が地味なばかりに…
explain: Expresses regret that a bad result came about only because of that cause.
examples: 1. あの飛行機に乗ったばかりに、彼は死んだ。
Just because he got on that plane, he died.
2. 英語の先生が嫌いなばかりに、英語も嫌いになってしまった。
Just because I disliked my English teacher, I ended up disliking English too.
mistakes: Using it for a good result: unnatural. For “努力したばかりに合格した” you should use “おかげで/だけに”.
Confusing it with ～せいで: the JLPT tests the “single cause” nuance of ～ばかりに.
Form: with Aな/N in formal style you need “であるばかりに”; avoid “だばかりに”.

rows: More neutral regarding “single cause”; ～ばかりに emphasizes “just because of that one reason”.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>のせいで<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れた。
Neutral/objective; lacks the strong tone of regret of ～ばかりに.
<ruby>渋滞<rt>じゅうたい</rt></ruby>のために<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れた。
The result usually matches expectations; with ～ばかりに the result is usually bad/unexpected.
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>しただけに<ruby>嬉<rt>うれ</rt></ruby>しい。
<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>りたいばかりに<ruby>聞<rt>ききだし</rt></ruby>き<ruby>出<rt></rt></ruby>した。

fields.connection: Vる + まい / Vます + まい (Group 2)
examples: I won't say anything more to him, since he won't listen to anyone's advice.
Even when I think I won't eat sweets anymore, I end up eating them anyway.
I will never again do something as stupid as chugging a drink in one go.
She turned her face away so as not to show her tears.
He looked really unwell yesterday, so he probably won't come to today's sports meet.
With rain at this level, there's probably no danger of the river flooding.
fields.explain:
Formal, leaning toward written language, speeches and reports; in conversation, ～ないだろう／～ないと思う is usually used.
Negative volition usually goes with volitional verbs and has the speaker as subject.
With N/な: use であるまい to keep a serious tone.

• Negative conjecture: “probably not/unlikely to …” (= ～ないだろう). Written, formal, sometimes classical.
• Negative volition: “determined not to/will never …” when the speaker tells themselves, showing strong resolve.
• “～まいと（して）” means “trying not to …”. “～まいか” is used as a rhetorical question, emphasizing an affirmative expectation.
fields.notes:
• In natural spoken language, switch to: きっと来ない／来ないと思う to avoid sounding stiff.
• “すまい” exists but is rarely used; “するまい” is more common.
• “あるまい” is used with ある (e.g., そんなことはあるまい = there's probably no such thing). meaning_vi: determined not to, intend not to ⏐ explain: Firmly wanting to give up ～ (expresses negative volition)
A formal expression used in written language.
The sentence is stiff.
⏐ examples: 1. あんなひどいところ、二度と行くまい。
A terrible place like that—I'm determined never to go there again.
2. 海外旅行では、絶対に買った水以外は飲むまいと思った。
When traveling abroad, I resolved never to drink any water other than water I had bought. explain: Expresses negative conjecture.
A formal expression used in written language.
The sentence is stiff. ⏐ examples: 1. 彼には私の気持ちはわかるまい。
He probably won't understand my feelings.
2. 上級者でも、この問題はできまい。
Even advanced learners probably can't solve this problem.
3. 夢ではあるまいか。
Could this be a dream?
mistakes: Wrong Group 2 conjugation: × 食べるまい → ○ 食べまい（drop ます: 食べます → 食べ）
Using it in everyday conversation makes the sentence stiff; the JLPT often tests the natural replacement ～ないだろう.
Confusing the “volition” meaning with “conjecture”: use the context, subject and person to tell them apart.
Mistaking “すまい” for the polite form: it is actually an old variant of するまい.

rows: Neutral, lacks the strong resolve of ～まい
Expresses an effort to avoid doing something

examples: You must not hurt people by giving in to your emotions.
I wandered around town wherever my feet took me.
I ended up signing just as I was told to.
Please leave these documents as they are.
I fell asleep with the TV left on.
Please state your opinion as you see fit.
fields.explain:
N/ V-る + ままに: “following/letting be”, may imply a lack of control or deliberately letting go.
V-た + ままに（しておく）/ そのままに: emphasizes maintaining a state; often used in instructions and operations.
In written language/formal expression, “言われるがままに/成り行きのままに” creates a nuance of being swept along.
Avoid overusing “ままに” when the meaning is purely “exactly as/identical to” → in that case “とおり（に）/どおり（に）” is more natural.

• Meaning 1: “Just as…, letting…, led by…” → emphasizes that the action happens following emotions, wishes or circumstances without resisting. Example: 感情のままに話す.
• Meaning 2: “Keeping a state unchanged” when used with V-た + ままにする/しておく or そのままに（しておく）. Example: ドアを開けたままにしておく.
• Difference in nuance:

V-るままに/Nのままに: going along, letting be (more or less a passive nuance of following emotions/circumstances).
V-たままに（しておく）: maintaining a state that has occurred → neutral or negative depending on the context.

• V-るままに/Nのままに: going along, letting be (more or less a passive nuance of following emotions/circumstances).
• V-たままに（しておく）: maintaining a state that has occurred → neutral or negative depending on the context.
• “〜がままに” is a variant with the nuance “exactly as told, being led”.
fields.notes:
• “ありのままに” is a fixed phrase meaning “as it is, just as it naturally is”.
• “V-るがままに” is somewhat literary: 風の吹くがままに, 波の赴くがままに.
• For operating machines/procedures, “そのままにしておく” is safe and neutral; when describing attitudes/behavior, use “Nのままに/V-るままに”. | Meaning: doing as one is made to (causative sense) (Vられるまま(に))
mistakes: Confusing “〜ままに” with “〜とおりに”: when you want to say “exactly according to the instructions/standard” → とおりに/どおりに is more natural.
Missing “に” in the state-keeping structure with operation verbs: use “V-たままにしておく/にする”.
Using “V-るままに” for the neutral meaning “exactly as” → unnatural; switch to “とおりに”.
It may appear on JLPT N2-N1 with the nuance of “being swept along”: 言われるがままに＝passive, you need to recognize it.

examples: I got angry one-sidedly without any regard for the other person's feelings, and I regret it.
Without caring that she was getting wet in the rain, she ran after him.
When the mother heard her son was safe, she cried out loud without caring who saw.
*Throwing trash anywhere without caring where. Working without caring how one looks.
She burst into tears without caring who was watching.
He ran to the station without caring that he was getting wet in the rain.
fields.explain:
Placed right after the element being ignored:人目もかまわず, ルールもかまわず.
The nuance is usually negative or one of surprise; be careful when the subject is “I/we” to avoid putting yourself down.
Rarely used in direct command/request sentences.

• Expresses behavior of “not caring, paying no attention” to something one should care about (rules, people's eyes, weather, circumstances…).
• Usually carries the speaker's evaluation (surprise, criticism); rarely used for commands/the listener's volition.
• Different from “にもかかわらず”: “もかまわず” emphasizes that the agent actively ignores/doesn't care; “にもかかわらず” only shows a fact contrary to expectation and is more neutral.
fields.notes:
• Often used with nouns of a social nature: 人目, 迷惑, マナー, ルール, 時間, 年齢, 体裁.
• In spoken language, “の” can be dropped when the nominalized phrase is short, but in written language you should keep “〜のもかまわず”.
• Often goes with sudden/instinctive actions: 泣き出す, 叫ぶ, 走る, 電話する.
mistakes: Using it in request/command sentences: × 人目もかまわず歌ってください → unnatural.
Confusing it with “にもかかわらず”: test questions set traps by changing the agent to see whether there is a nuance of “deliberately ignoring”.
Forgetting “の” when nominalizing a verb: × 濡れるもかまわず → ✓ 濡れるのもかまわず.

examples: I never even imagined I would be told something like that.
The company president, without even looking carefully, says, "This is no good at all. Rewrite the whole thing again."
If you keep playing games without even eating, you'll get sick.
You're going to give up from the start, without even trying to see whether you can do it?

A: I messed up. This shirt is a bit too flashy.
B: That's because you bought it without even looking carefully.
fields.explain: ◎ An expression that emphasizes the negative form of 「それも～ない」.

examples: You shouldn't laugh at people in front of others.
Parents shouldn't force their own preferences on their children.
Important information is not something you should show to others casually.
Life is not something that can be bought with money.
Laughing at other people's failures is not acceptable.
One shouldn't say such things
fields.explain:
Used to state a view as a principle, not aimed directly at an individual like a command.
Usually takes a general subject (人は/子どもは/約束は…).
In conversation it sounds soft but still serious: it has a tone of “admonishing”.

• Admonishing, stating a moral/social rule: “one should not do…”.
• Stating a general judgment of impossibility: “cannot/is not something to…”.
• Objective, impersonal nuance; often used in written language and in statements of principle.
fields.notes:
• When criticizing a specific behavior of the other person, ものではない makes the sentence less harsh than てはいけない.
• Besides “should not”, many sentences are naturally translated as “is not something…”, “cannot…”.
• Often appears in JLPT questions to distinguish its nuance from べきではない/てはいけない.
mistakes: Confusing it with てはいけない (direct prohibition) → wrong choice when the sentence states a general principle.
Confusing it with ないほうがいい (personal advice) → when the sentence has a general subject “人は…”, prefer ものではない/べきではない.
Using the past tense before ものではない: × したものではない → it must be V辞書形.

examples: If I could redo my life, I would.
(To a sick child) If I could take your place, I would.
If I could, I'd love to try delicacies from all over the world.
If it were possible to stop the destruction of nature, I would want to stop it by any means.
*"There's no way you can jump down from somewhere this high. Go ahead and try it if you think you can."
If I could go home, I'd go back to my hometown right now.
fields.explain:
Usually used with potential verbs (戻れる、できる、会える…).
The second clause expresses the speaker's wish/intention/evaluation.
In the challenging usage, the second clause is usually ～てみろ／てごらん (strong/mild).
Standard/written in tone, not very colloquial except when used as a challenge.

• An almost unreal supposition (counterfactual/low probability): “if only one could…/I wish…”.
• Used to express a strong desire or regret, or to state a condition that is hard to meet.
• Challenging variant: a harsh/provoking nuance, usually in spoken language.
fields.notes:
• In translation: “if only…”, “if it were possible… then…”, “if you think you can, then go ahead and…”.
• The JLPT often tests the difference between ～ものなら (hard-to-realize supposition) and ～ようものなら (bad consequence).
• The implied subject is usually the speaker or the other person (in the challenging usage).
mistakes: Confusing it with ～たら (feasible) → wrong choice when the context is “unlikely/far-fetched”.
Confusing it with ～ようものなら (bad consequence) → look at the second clause: wish vs. warning.
Using it awkwardly with adjectives/nouns: this pattern is mainly used with verbs.

examples: I joined a sports club, but I've only been once so far.
I tried walking around the hotel, but there was nothing interesting.
Although I know cigarettes are bad for my health, I just can't quit.
Although I graduated from university, I can't find a job.
That student has good grades, but their attitude toward studying is not good.
Although this furniture has a delicate and elegant design, it can't really be called practical.
fields.explain:
Usually used when reality does not match what one would logically expect from the first clause.
In spoken language the second clause can be dropped to imply something: ～ものの…。 (implying “but…”)
Avoid attaching a direct command/suggestion in the second clause.

• Concession, “although… but…”, expresses a result/state contrary to what was expected from the first clause.
• More formal than ～が／～けれど(も); often used in writing, journalism and reports.
• The second clause is usually not a direct command/request, but a fact/evaluation.
fields.notes:
• If the second clause is a suggestion, use ～が／～けれど instead of ものの to sound more natural.
• In formal writing, であるものの/とはいうものの appear frequently.
• Translate flexibly: “although… ,”, “though… , still…”. explain: Used to express something unexpected, an exception that often happens. ⏐ examples: 1. 車の免許は持っているものの、ほとんど運転したことがない。
I have a driver's license, but I've hardly ever driven.
2. 申し込みはしたものの、試験を受けるかどうか未定だ。
I've applied, but I haven't decided yet whether to take the exam.
3. 春とはいうものの、まだ寒い。
Although it's spring, it's still cold.
mistakes: Using ものの with a command/suggestion: × 予約はしたものの、来てください。→ unnatural.
Confusing it with のに (which has a nuance of reproach): test questions often set traps with emotion.
Dropping 「である」 with nouns/な-adjectives in formal writing → unnatural.
